claims.text: Rapid solidification produces a homogeneous, supersaturated single-phase Mg-containing lightweight HEA.
The proposed alloy has a density below 6 g/cm³.
High-temperature exposure drives diffusion-mediated phase separation of the metastable supersaturated alloy.
Prolonged exposure to chloride solution at room temperature can induce phase separation in the alloy.
Phase separation involves segregation and nucleation of stable Ti-rich or Mg-stabilized intermetallic compounds.
The intermetallic compounds preferentially segregate or grow at grain boundaries and defect sites.
The precipitated intermetallic phases alter local chemical potentials and oxide-formation kinetics.
Intermetallic phases promote a protective passivating oxide by reducing microgalvanic coupling or supplying beneficial elements such as Ti to the scale.
The phase evolution improves corrosion resistance relative to the as-cast state.
The phase evolution improves high-temperature oxidation behavior relative to the as-cast state.
Aged samples will have a larger secondary-intermetallic phase fraction, particularly at grain boundaries.
Aged samples will exhibit a more noble corrosion potential and lower corrosion current density than the as-cast baseline.
Aged samples will form thicker or more adherent oxide scales during high-temperature oxidation.
The proposed evolution requires sufficient diffusivity and environmental exposure capable of enabling phase separation.
The identity and volume fraction of intermetallic phases, and the magnitude of corrosion and oxidation changes, may vary with alloy composition and processing.
XRD and SEM/EDS can be used to compare phase composition and intermetallic fraction between aged and as-cast samples.
Potentiodynamic polarization and oxidation-scale characterization provide controlled comparisons of corrosion and oxidation behavior.
